papers.title: Chromatin and transcriptional dynamics associated with seasonal growth across a latitudinal Cline in birch.
papers.abstract: Seasonal growth-dormancy cycles determine the survival and distribution of trees, yet the chromatin and transcriptional changes associated with contrasting seasonal growth patterns in forest trees remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigated chromatin regulation and transcriptional changes during seasonal growth in birch, focusing on changes that may link photoperiod responses to circadian regulation and bud-set. We combined satellite-derived phenology from 96 Betula platyphylla (B. platyphylla) forest stands with a common-garden comparison of mid-latitude B. platyphylla and high-latitude B. pendula material established in 2008 and phenologically monitored from 2020. Seasonal buds were profiled across an annual cycle by RNA-seq and CUT&Tag for H3K4me3/H3K27me3. Diurnal RNA-seq across key months quantified circadian phase/amplitude changes. The contribution of BpREF6 to growth cessation and bud-set progression was investigated by assessing growth-cessation and bud-set progression under short-day conditions and profiling histone modifications in CRISPR/Cas9-edited B. platyphylla plants. Across natural stands, end-of-season timing and growing-season length were strongly associated with daylength, whereas temperature showed limited explanatory power for end of season (EOS). In the common garden, provenances shared similar bud break timing but differed markedly in bud set, consistent with photoperiod thresholds. Multi-omics analyses revealed extensive seasonal and between-provenance chromatin-state differences, with enriched REF6 motifs across chromatin states and pronounced divergence of BpREF6 expression during the transition to bud set. Network and diurnal analyses suggested that circadian- and photoperiod-related genes, including PRR5/PRR7, CCA1/LHY, TOC1, CO and FT, may participate in the BpREF6-associated regulatory network. bpref6 mutants showed accelerated bud-set progression and earlier observed growth cessation than control under short-day conditions, accompanied by an increased number of H3K27me3 peaks, lower H3K4me3 signals at the analyzed regions, and altered chromatin and transcriptional profiles at selected circadian-, photoperiod-, and growth cessation-related genes. Some transcriptional changes in bpref6 resembled those observed in high-latitude birch during bud-set. Because BpREF6 occupancy was not profiled by ChIP-seq, these chromatin and transcriptional changes cannot be assigned as direct BpREF6 effects or distinguished from indirect consequences of the mutation and altered developmental state. Our findings reveal associations between photoperiod and seasonal phenology and identify BpREF6 as a chromatin-associated contributor to short-day-induced bud-set progression. The accompanying changes in histone modifications and circadian- and photoperiod-related transcriptional programs provide a framework for further investigating how chromatin regulation contributes to seasonal growth and latitude-associated growth cessation variation in birch.

papers.title: Ocular Static Fixation as a Sign of Delirium.
papers.abstract: Ocular motor behavior (OMB) has been proposed as a delirium marker. To analyze the discriminant value of ocular static fixation (OSF) and saccadic eye movements (SEM) in delirium diagnosis and their relationship to delirium phenomenology using the Delirium Rating Scale-Revised-98 (DRS-R98). Cross-sectional bedside evaluation of OSF and four SEM tests in 223 consecutive geriatric inpatients, with or without DSM-5-TR delirium. Logistic regressions assessed performance of OMB for delirium diagnosis while controlling for clinical confounds and contribution of OMB to delirium and its three core domains. Correlational analysis assessed the relationship between OMB and DRS-R98 core domains and overall severity. All OMB tests had higher specificity than sensitivity, with better positive than negative likelihood ratios. OSF, saccadic initiation delay and hypometria, as well as saccadic initiation failure, were delirium discriminants in logistic models with age, neuroleptics and drowsiness as control variables. The logistic model for OSF had the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC 91.6%). Only OSF contributed to delirium diagnosis when identified together with each of three core delirium symptoms (sleep-wake cycle, attention, thought process; 90.1%-93.7% logistic models' AUC). OMB were not correlated with delirium motor subtypes or core domains. Saccadic initiation failure's (n=16) association with delirium was a nonspecific inability to be tested. OSF had the best performance for delirium presence. It is easily assessed at the bedside and simpler than SEM for patient cooperation. Its high specificity suggests a role to combine it with high sensitivity brief delirium tools.
papers.journal: Journal of the Academy of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry

papers.title: Perceived sleep disruption and opioid consumption in chronic low back pain: Craving as a mediating pathway.
papers.abstract: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) affects more than 600 million people worldwide, many of whom receive long-term opioid therapy (LTOT). Sleep disturbance, particularly wake after sleep onset (WASO), may contribute to opioid craving and use, yet the temporal relationships among WASO, craving, and opioid dose in chronic pain populations remain poorly understood. Adults with CLBP receiving LTOT (N = 81) completed 14 days of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and overnight actigraphy monitoring. WASO was assessed using sleep diaries and overnight actigraphy, while morning and nocturnal craving, pain severity, and daily opioid dose (morphine milligram equivalents) were assessed using EMA. Linear mixed-effects models examined main and interactive effects of WASO and pain severity on craving and opioid dose. Multilevel mediation models tested whether craving mediated the relationship between WASO and opioid dose. Greater diary-based WASO was associated with higher nocturnal opioid craving. Pain severity emerged as a strong predictor of both nocturnal and morning craving and moderated the association between WASO and opioid dose, such that greater WASO was associated with higher opioid dose on high-pain days. Mediation analyses demonstrated significant indirect effects of WASO on opioid dose through both nocturnal and morning craving. Exploratory analyses using actigraphy-derived WASO showed minimal associations with craving or opioid dose. Perceived sleep disruption was associated with opioid craving and opioid consumption among individuals with CLBP receiving LTOT. Craving may represent a cognitive-affective pathway linking disrupted sleep to opioid use, highlighting sleep disturbance as a potentially modifiable intervention target in chronic pain populations.

papers.title: Interfloor noise triggers sleep fragmentation and affective deficits via dysregulation of the orexin-serotonin axis and hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
papers.abstract: Residential interfloor noise is an urban stressor with unknown neurobiological effects on sleep and mood. This study aimed to elucidate the effects of interfloor noise on sleep architecture, affective behavior, and molecular biomarkers using a mouse model. The post-exposure sleep-wake states of male C57BL/6 mice exposed to simulated interfloor noise (70-100 dB) for 12 h daily for 7 days were monitored via piezoelectric sensing, which was followed by behavioral tests for anxiety- and depression-like phenotypes. Molecular analyses were performed to quantify neuroendocrine, neuroinflammatory, neurotransmitter, and synaptic plasticity markers in the hypothalamus and hippocampus. Exploratory hippocampal RNA-seq was used to assess transcriptomic alterations. Seven days of interfloor noise exposure induced sleep fragmentation (increased bout frequency and shortened duration) and selectively reduced REM sleep while preserving total and NREM sleep. Mice exposed to interfloor noise exhibited anxiety-like behaviors and behavioral despair, and molecularly, they had increased hypothalamic cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and interleukin-1β) and decreased serum corticosterone. Interfloor noise induced hypothalamic orexin-serotonin dysregulation, increased hippocampal GABAergic signaling, and reduced hippocampal HTR1A, HTR2A, BDNF, PSD95, and p-ERK expression. Hypothalamic markers were correlated with sleep disruption, whereas hippocampal markers were correlated with anxiety. RNA-seq revealed the upregulation of Hif3a and oxygen response transcriptomic changes, indicating an additional hippocampal stress response. The 7-day interfloor noise paradigm provides a valid mouse model for REM sleep disruption, fragmentation, and mood deficits. This study offers a platform for future mechanistic and interventional studies of interfloor noise-induced disorders.

papers.title: Sleep as a vulnerability marker in clinical high-risk populations. a multimodal systematic review.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as clinically significant features of the psychosis risk state, yet no comprehensive synthesis has examined sleep across all assessment modalities in clinical high-risk (CHR) populations. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, five major databases were searched (January 1995-March 2026) for original studies assessing sleep in CHR populations, with CHR status operationalized through validated instruments. From 5218 citations, 26 studies were included. Sleep disturbances affected 59-80% of CHR individuals. Actigraphy predicted positive symptom worsening at 12-month follow-up. Experience sampling identified nocturnal awakenings as predictors of next-day paranoia and derealization, mediated by morning negative affect. Sleep disturbance predicted symptom severity over time, accelerated transition among converters, and was independently associated with suicidal ideation. High-density EEG polysomnography documented reduced prefrontal spindle duration, elevated non-rapid eye movement (NREM) gamma power, and reduced slow wave density - replicated across independent cohorts. A multimodal neuroimaging study identified whole-thalamus-dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) hypoconnectivity as a convergent thalamocortical marker. Sleep disturbances in CHR populations span multiple neurobiologically distinct domains. Polysomnographic markers - spindle parameters and NREM gamma power - represent the most neurophysiologically specific signatures identified. Standardized sleep assessment should be integrated into CHR clinical protocols as both a prognostic tool and a modifiable therapeutic target.

papers.title: EEG responses to monosodium glutamate concentration and individual umami sensitivity in healthy adults.
papers.abstract: Taste perception depends on stimulus intensity and individual sensitivity, but how these factors shape cortical responses to monosodium glutamate (MSG) is unclear. We combined psychophysics and 64-channel EEG in 38 healthy adults grouped by MSG detection threshold. Increasing MSG concentration reduced fronto-central P200 and posterior N200 amplitudes (FDR-corrected p < .001; partial η2 = 0.30-0.50), and evoked beta power was highest at the lowest concentration. Exploratory source analyses showed weaker right orbitofrontal-dorsolateral prefrontal beta-band (14-30 Hz) connectivity at higher concentrations. The ERP effects were robust to alternative preprocessing. No group effect survived correction, and sensitivity could not be decoded above chance. Lower detection thresholds were associated with larger posterior late positive potentials (exploratory). EEG captures robust neural responses to MSG concentration and may complement sensory panels, whereas neural markers of individual sensitivity require larger samples.

papers.title: Abnormal SEP recovery amongst multimodal electrophysiological studies to indicate cortical dysfunction in PME.
papers.abstract: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (PMEs) are rare neurodegenerative disorders characterized by cortical hyperexcitability and progressive neurological deterioration. We aimed to identify electrophysiological markers of cortical dysfunction using multimodal neurophysiological assessment. Seventeen adult PME patients underwent clinical evaluation and video-EEG recording. Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEP), SEP recovery function and surround inhibition, blink reflex, and motor evoked potentials (MEP) were assessed in 11 patients and compared with 11 matched healthy controls. Generalized epileptiform discharges were observed in all patients. SEP recordings demonstrated increased N20/P25 amplitudes and prolonged P14, N18, and P25 latencies. SEP recovery showed marked attenuation at the shortest interstimulus interval followed by rapid amplitude recovery. Surround inhibition was preserved. Blink reflex studies revealed prolonged R2 latencies and increased amplitudes. MEP parameters did not differ significantly between groups. PME is associated with abnormal SEP recovery dynamics and giant SEPs, consistent with impaired somatosensory inhibitory processing. Blink reflex abnormalities suggest additional subcortical involvement, whereas corticospinal excitability appears relatively preserved.

papers.title: Evaluating the impact of hypoglossal nerve stimulator therapy on cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes in sleep apnea patients: A retrospective cohort analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea is associated with comorbidities such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. While continuous positive airway pressure therapy has been shown to improve these conditions, the impact of hypoglossal nerve stimulation remains less defined. This retrospective cohort study aimed to evaluate the effect of hypoglossal nerve stimulation on blood pressure, mean arterial pressure, hemoglobin A1c, and body mass index in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Adult patients who underwent hypoglossal nerve stimulator implantation between February 2017 and June 2024 at a tertiary academic medical center were included. Exclusion criteria included device removal, transfer of care following activation, or loss to follow-up. Of 210 patients, 141 met inclusion criteria, with age ranging 18 to 87 years, and 60.3% male. Over a two-year follow-up, systolic and diastolic blood pressures fluctuated without reaching statistical significance, while mean arterial pressure demonstrated a downward trend that approached significance at the two-year time point. Hemoglobin A1c and body mass index also varied over time without significant change. The mean Apnea-Hypopnea Index improved substantially from 36.0 at baseline to 5.9 at titration follow-up, and overall institutional compliance with hypoglossal nerve stimulation therapy was 83.5%. In this cohort, hypoglossal nerve stimulation significantly improved obstructive sleep apnea severity but did not result in significant changes in blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c, or body mass index. The observed trend toward lower mean arterial pressure suggests a potential cardiovascular benefit, warranting further investigation into the broader metabolic effects of hypoglossal nerve stimulation in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.

papers.title: Postoperative changes in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis following adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy and sleep-disordered breathing: A prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis (PMNE) and sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) may coexist in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Improvement in enuresis has been reported after upper-airway surgery performed for sleep-related indications, but the surgery-specific contribution remains uncertain because PMNE may improve spontaneously and published studies are heterogeneous. To evaluate changes in PMNE and daytime sleepiness from baseline to 3 months following adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy in children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy and clinically diagnosed SDB. This uncontrolled prospective cohort study included 140 children aged 5-11 years with clinically diagnosed PMNE who underwent adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy between 2023 and 2025 after meeting otorhinolaryngologic criteria for upper-airway surgery. PMNE was clinically diagnosed by pediatric urology according to ICCS and EAU-ESPU criteria. SDB was diagnosed clinically; routine polysomnography was not performed. Weekly wet-night frequency and modified Epworth Sleepiness Scale (mESS) scores were recorded at baseline and 3 months postoperatively. Complete response was defined as no wet nights at 3 months. Factors associated with complete response were explored using multivariable logistic regression. Median wet-night frequency decreased from 3 (IQR, 2-7) to 0 (IQR, 0-2) nights/week, with a median within-participant reduction of 2 (IQR, 2-3; P < 0.001). The complementary mean reduction was 2.74 nights/week (95% CI, 2.41-3.08). Median mESS score decreased from 4 (IQR, 3-5) to 2 (IQR, 0-3; P < 0.001). At 3 months, 74 children (52.9%) had complete response, 42 (30.0%) had partial response, and 24 (17.1%) had no benefit. Higher baseline wet-night frequency was associated with lower odds of complete response (7 vs 2 nights/week: adjusted OR, 0.08; 95% CI, 0.02-0.26; P < 0.001), whereas age and surgical procedure were not independently associated with complete response. A substantial subset of this carefully phenotyped cohort improved during the 3-month postoperative period. However, the absence of a non-operative comparator prevents separation of changes temporally associated with surgery from spontaneous remission, regression to the mean, or other time-related influences. The lack of routine polysomnography also precluded objective grading of SDB severity, and the 3-month follow-up does not establish durable remission. In children with PMNE and clinically diagnosed SDB who had already met otorhinolaryngologic criteria for upper-airway surgery, short-term improvement in wet-night frequency and daytime sleepiness was observed after surgery. These findings do not quantify a surgery-specific treatment effect and do not support adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy solely for PMNE. Controlled prospective studies with objective SDB assessment and longer follow-up are required.

papers.title: Time-of-Day Variation in Airway Hyperresponsiveness in Asthma: Potential Circadian Mechanisms and Translational Implications.
papers.abstract: Airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) is a key physiological feature of asthma and contributes to excessive airway narrowing in response to diverse stimuli. Although asthma-related airway physiology exhibits marked temporal variation, whether AHR itself is independently regulated by the endogenous circadian clock remains unclear. In this narrative review, we summarize current evidence on the definition and temporal phenotype of AHR, with particular emphasis on distinguishing clock-time variation from endogenous circadian regulation and on direct evidence from bronchial provocation studies. We further discuss potential mechanisms linking circadian biology to AHR, including neuroendocrine and autonomic gating, epithelial-immune temporal coupling, airway smooth muscle reactivity, and metabolic and redox regulation. Current evidence supports substantial time dependence of asthma-related airway physiology, whereas direct evidence for an intrinsic circadian rhythm of AHR in humans remains limited with mechanistic insights derived predominantly from animal, ex vivo, and cellular studies. We also review time-dependent treatment strategies, particularly inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) administration, while distinguishing clinically investigated dosing schedules from experimental clock-targeted interventions. Overall, circadian biology provides a framework for understanding temporal variation in AHR and may inform future approaches to phenotyping and treatment timing; however, circadian-based AHR management and clock-targeted therapies remain investigational and require validation in well-controlled human studies.

papers.title: Wearable Technologies to Improve Physical Activity, Sedentary Breaks, Training, Sleep, and Safety: The ECSS-Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group Calls for Interdisciplinary Collaboration.
papers.abstract: Wearable technologies ("wearables") are lightweight sensor-based devices that detect, analyze, and transmit physiological, biomechanical or environmental data, and are increasingly used across physical activity, sedentary behavior, athletic training, safety and sleep research. Applications include for example large-scale physical activity surveillance, ambulatory assessment, and real-time feedback during athletic training. Despite promising use cases such as heart rate variability-informed endurance training or gait retraining via biomechanical feedback, critical challenges remain. These include insufficient data quality, inadequately evaluated and inaccessible algorithms, limited interoperability between systems, difficulties translating sensor data into actionable insights, and insufficient wearable technology literacy among users. The Wearable Technologies Special Interest Group of the European College of Sport Science (ECSS-WT-SIG) identifies the need for interdisciplinary collaboration to address these challenges. Key priorities include developing regulatory frameworks, promoting standardized and open data infrastructure, improving wearable literacy of users, and conducting rigorous intervention studies under real-world conditions. The ECSS-WT-SIG calls on researchers, industry partners, NGOs, and other stakeholders to collectively advance the scientific and practical application of wearables in physical activity, sedentary behavior, training, sleep, and safety research.

papers.title: A Current Evidence Review From the Italian Society of Pediatric Allergology and Immunology (SIAIP) on Practical Management of Allergic Rhinitis in Children and Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is highly prevalent in children and adolescents and impairs quality of life, sleep, and school performance, while also worsening asthma control. The last EAACI position paper on pediatric AR was published in 2013. Significant scientific advancements, including the new ARIA 2026 guidelines, necessitate an updated national framework. This Italian Society of Pediatric Allergology and Immunology (SIAIP) document aims to provide an evidence-based age-specific framework for the diagnosis, classification, and practical management of AR in children and adolescents, while addressing the limitations of existing less granular guidelines. A dedicated SIAIP experts' board reviewed current scientific literature, integrated updated epidemiological data, revised classifications, and emerging evidence on allergen immunotherapy. It incorporates the ARIA 2026 guidelines and adapts them to the clinical challenges and age-specific considerations relevant to pediatric practice. The board of qualified experts and a panel of multidisciplinary clinicians discussed and approved the document. This document covers the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and diagnosis of AR in children and adolescents. It provides detailed stepwise pharmacologic recommendations and discusses the role of allergen immunotherapy (AIT), taking age-specific factors and complementary therapies into account. Evidence-based statements and practical management algorithms aim to optimize diagnostic pathways and therapeutic interventions. This SIAIP document offers clinically actionable guidance for healthcare professionals. It emphasizes early diagnosis, stepwise treatment strategies, and the disease-modifying role of AIT, aiming to enhance diagnostic accuracy, streamline management, and ultimately improve the long-term health and well-being of affected children and adolescents.

papers.title: CalDyn: an advanced high-throughput automated algorithm for monitoring intracellular calcium dynamics and electrophysiological signals in patient-derived cells.
papers.abstract: Quantitative analysis of intracellular calcium and electrophysiological signals is challenging when signals exhibit baseline drift, low-amplitude events, irregular waveforms, or multicomponent transients. We developed CalDyn, a MATLAB-based graphical application for automated peak detection, waveform characterization, event classification, batch processing, quality control and data export. CalDyn combines Savitzky-Golay filtering, LOESS-assisted derivative detection, optional baseline correction, waveform-boundary fitting and rule-based peak classification. It was evaluated on calcium recordings (healthy and disease-associated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, hiPSC-derived neurons, primary skeletal myotubes), current-clamp action potentials and cardiac optical-mapping signals. Outputs were compared with PeakInspector, Clampfit and BV Workbench using paired and Bland-Altman analyses. Detection was assessed against 142 expert-annotated events and synthetic signals of known timing and amplitude. CalDyn achieved 94.4% sensitivity, 89.9% precision and an F1 score of 0.92. Performance peaked for healthy cardiomyocytes, paced myotubes and action potentials, with lower recall in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes and variable precision in neurons. CalDyn detected candidate low-amplitude diastolic and multicomponent Ca2+ events in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes, although the biological identity of CalDyn-only events was not independently confirmed. Comparisons with software revealed parameter-specific systematic differences, notably for rise rates and classifications. Action-potential measurements showed limited mean bias but non-negligible limits of agreement. In synthetic signals, amplitude error increased with noise and uncorrected drift, and timing error with low sampling rates. Detection remained stable across moderate parameter variation. CalDyn provides an accessible, reproducible and versatile workflow for automated analysis of heterogeneous calcium and electrophysiological signals. With appropriate quality control, it offers a robust alternative to modality-specific tools.

papers.title: Sensorimotor expertise effects extend from dance to face perception.
papers.abstract: Domain specific expertise affects neural and behavioral processes of perception and memory. We explore if sensorimotor expertise extends to other relevant social mechanisms, such as the neural processing of emotional faces. We recorded brain activity of 26 dancers and 26 non-dancers using visual and somatosensory evoked potentials (VEPs, SEPs) during an emotion and sex discrimination task on happy, afraid, and neutral faces. We predicted expertise-related modulation of visual facial emotion processing in visual and somatosensory areas. EEG results revealed distinct visual and somatosensory ERP patterns in the two groups. VEP findings showed that dancers distinguished between neutral and emotional faces at N170 and P200. Non-dancers differentiated between the three emotions with more lateralized processing. For SEPs, dancers uniquely showed early emotion effects (P50) in central somatosensory regions and task-modulated somatosensory engagement at later stages (N80, P100). Non-dancers showed later, localized somatosensory effects. In summary, dance expertise shapes both visual and somatosensory processing of facial emotion, indicating a broader neural representation of emotions. These findings provide novel evidence for a differential facial emotion processing in dancers, extending the dance expertise modulation beyond perception of dance-specific stimuli, to face emotion perception. Overall, this work highlights the strong influence of sensorimotor training on emotion perception.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythm-Associated Diagnostic Biomarkers Reveal Immune Dysregulation and Molecular Subtypes in Recurrent Pregnancy Loss.
papers.abstract: Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) is a clinically complex reproductive disorder involving impaired maternal-fetal communication and immune imbalance. Circadian rhythm disturbance has recently attracted attention in reproductive failure, but its diagnostic relevance and possible connection with immune dysregulation in RPL remain insufficiently defined. GSE165004 was used as the discovery cohort, and GSE26787 was used as an independent small cohort for preliminary evaluation. Circadian rhythm-associated genes were collected from GeneCards. Differential expression analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and ssGSEA-based circadian rhythm scoring were integrated to identify RPL-associated circadian transcriptional alterations. Candidate genes were further evaluated by protein-protein interaction analysis, functional enrichment, receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, nomogram construction, immune infiltration assessment, molecular subtype identification, and ceRNA regulatory network prediction. RPL samples showed a significantly lower circadian rhythm-associated gene score than control samples, indicating reduced circadian-associated transcriptional activity. Three genes, GJA1, UCP2, and GSN, were identified as circadian rhythm-associated candidate diagnostic biomarkers for RPL. In the discovery cohort, the AUC values of GJA1, UCP2, and GSN were 0.80, 0.77, and 0.81, respectively. Their diagnostic performance was further evaluated in an independent small cohort, where the AUC values were 0.72, 0.80, and 0.92, respectively. GSN showed a significant expression difference between RPL and control samples in the independent cohort, whereas GJA1 and UCP2 did not reach statistical significance. Immune infiltration analysis revealed changes in fibroblast, neutrophil, macrophage, Treg, T helper cell, and interferon-related signatures. Consensus clustering based on the three biomarkers classified RPL samples into two molecular subtypes with different immune-stromal characteristics, coagulation-related activity, and metabolic features. The ceRNA network contained 3 diagnostic mRNAs, 43 predicted miRNAs, and 61 upstream lncRNAs. GJA1, UCP2, and GSN may represent circadian rhythm-associated candidate biomarkers for RPL. Their expression patterns may reflect circadian-immune dysregulation and molecular heterogeneity. These findings provide a circadian rhythm-based perspective for understanding RPL pathogenesis and nominate candidate molecules for future diagnostic and mechanistic validation.

papers.title: Effect of two-jaw orthognathic surgery on pharyngeal airway and sleep parameters in skeletal Class III patients with high-risk airways.
papers.abstract: Orthognathic surgery in skeletal Class III patients may alter upper airway morphology, particularly when posterior airway space is limited. This study evaluated changes in pharyngeal airway volume and sleep-related parameters after bimaxillary surgery and assessed postoperative hyoid bone displacement in patients with high-risk airways (posterior airway space ≤ 11 mm). A prospective single-arm, pre-post interventional study was conducted between 2022 and 2024 at a university hospital. Fourteen adults (9 women, 5 men; mean age 25.36 ± 4.73 years) without prior obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) underwent Le Fort I advancement and bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomy. Cone-beam computed tomography was performed preoperatively (T0), immediately postoperatively (T1), and at 6 months (T2). Pharyngeal airway volume and hyoid position were measured. Sleep parameters included apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), STOP-BANG, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction was applied (P < 0.05). Mean maxillary advancement was 2 mm and mandibular setback 7.13 mm. Hypopharyngeal volume decreased significantly from T0 to T1 and T2 (P = 0.046), while nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal volumes showed no significant change. Hyoid position shifted posteriorly and inferiorly (P < 0.05). Sleep parameters remained within normal ranges with no new OSA cases. In this cohort, bimaxillary surgery with moderate mandibular setback was not associated with the development of OSA in Class III patients with anatomically high-risk airways. Hypopharyngeal volume remained significantly reduced at 6 months, and the hyoid remained posteriorly displaced, without corresponding changes in sleep parameters.

papers.title: Cerebral Blood Flow-Derived Myogenic Dynamics Reveal Impaired Postischemic Cerebrovascular Recovery in Experimental Stroke.
papers.abstract: Restoration of cerebral blood flow (CBF) after ischemic stroke does not necessarily indicate recovery of cerebrovascular regulation. We tested whether myogenic-band dynamics derived directly from CBF signals provide information beyond mean perfusion during cerebral ischemia and after acute stroke. Transient focal cerebral ischemia was induced in 29 Sprague-Dawley rats using middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion. Bilateral laser-Doppler flowmetry (LDF)-derived CBF signals were decomposed using empirical mode decomposition and Hilbert transform, and myogenic-band activity (0.15-0.4 Hz) was quantified by absolute and relative power. Cross-validated logistic regression models were used to evaluate whether myogenic-band power provided discriminative information beyond mean CBF alone. Ipsilateral mean CBF fell from 73.5±51.8 p.u. at baseline to 52.2±38.0 p.u. during late ischemia (P=0.0088), then increased to 126.6±91.5 p.u. after 3 hours of reperfusion (P=0.0050 versus baseline). Relative myogenic-band power decreased from 37.43±14.65% to 13.35±7.51% during ischemia (P<0.0001) and remained below baseline after reperfusion (20.74±12.02%, P=0.00033 versus baseline); contralateral relative power was comparatively preserved. Combining mean CBF and myogenic-band power improved discrimination of baseline from late ischemia (AUC, 0.99 versus 0.70 for mean CBF alone) and late reperfusion (AUC, 0.88 versus 0.70). Frequency-specific analysis of LDF-derived CBF reveals persistent, lateralized abnormalities in myogenic-band dynamics that are not captured by mean perfusion alone. The persistence of depressed myogenic activity despite restored or elevated mean CBF demonstrates incomplete recovery of frequency-specific oscillatory dynamics after reperfusion. These findings support myogenic-band power as a potential functional measure of persistent postischemic cerebrovascular dysfunction.

papers.title: Cardiac electrophysiology procedures must be performed exclusively by trained electrophysiologists: A statement from the Heart Rhythm Society and Heart Rhythm Advocates.
papers.abstract: The exponential growth of clinical cardiac electrophysiology (CCEP) as a subspecialty has created an important unresolved question in contemporary cardiovascular medicine: Who is qualified to perform electrophysiology (EP) procedures? As nonelectrophysiologists increasingly perform procedures that require the nuanced expertise of a trained or board-certified CCEP (eg, permanent pacemaker implantation, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation, cardiac resynchronization therapy, and transvenous lead extraction), the consequences for patient safety, procedural outcomes, and health system efficiency have become impossible to ignore. This article presents a comprehensive, evidence-based argument that cardiac EP procedures must be performed exclusively by physicians who have completed accredited fellowship training in CCEP. We draw upon peer-reviewed outcome data, guideline-derived training standards from the Heart Rhythm Society, the American College of Cardiology, and American Heart Association, including the newly published 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Rhythm Society Advanced Training Statement on Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology, as well as registry analyses spanning hundreds of thousands of patients to substantiate our position. The risks associated with suboptimal operator training are not theoretical; they are measurable, costly, and potentially fatal. The evidence presented demonstrates that operator specialization in EP is among the most powerful independent predictors of procedural safety and long-term outcomes and can be as important as institutional volume in many analyses. We call upon hospital credentialing committees, national medical societies, payers, regulatory bodies, and policymakers worldwide to establish and enforce a definitive standard: only trained CCEPs should implant and manage cardiac implantable electronic devices, perform catheter ablation procedures, execute transvenous lead extraction, and conduct formal EP studies.

papers.title: Objectively Measured Smartphone Use Is Associated With Worse Sleep Health Among Adolescents: The Stony Brook University MEDiA Study.
papers.abstract: Screen use among adolescents is ubiquitous and associated with poor sleep health. This study examined gender-specific associations between objectively measured smartphone use (including timing-specific and social-media-specific duration of use) and sleep health among a diverse national sample of adolescents. Adolescents (n = 218; 13-18 years old) from across the U.S. were recruited online. Participants (50% F) survey-reported sociodemographic characteristics, sleep timing, and sleep quality, and then installed a passive sensing meter on their personal smartphones (iOS or Android) for ≥3 days (M = 17.5) to objectively monitor smartphone activity, including app use, duration, and timing. Linear regression models assessed gender interactions in associations between timing- (i.e., 24-hour, evening 20:00-23:00, and nighttime 23:00-6:00) and category- (i.e., all-app or social media) specific smartphone use (hours/day) with nighttime sleep onset time, sleep duration, sleep quality, and sleep variability (social jetlag and free night catchup sleep), adjusting for sociodemographic and smartphone characteristics. Greater smartphone use was associated with later sleep onset time (b = 0.13-1.78 hours, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.07, 0.19-1.06, 2.51, β = 0.27-0.52), shorter sleep duration (b = -1.38 to -0.17 hours, 95% CI = -2.08, -0.72 to -0.25, -0.09, β = -0.48 to -0.36), more social jetlag (b = 0.06-0.43 hours, 95% CI = 0.01, 0.10-0.22, 0.64, β = 0.15-0.29), and longer free night catch-up sleep (b = 0.09-0.88 hours, 95% CI = 0.02, 0.17-0.38, 1.50, β = 0.16-0.29), with the strongest associations for evening, nighttime, and social media use. Several associations with sleep onset time and duration were stronger among females. The association between objectively assessed smartphone use and sleep health differs depending on timing and type of use and gender. Interventions to improve sleep health should consider aiming to reduce screen time around and after bedtime and social media specifically, which may especially benefit females.
papers.journal: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine

papers.title: The Effect of Exercise Training on Individuals With Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures significantly impair physical function and quality of life; however, evidence regarding the long-term effects of exercise interventions remains inconclusive. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of exercise training on pain, quality of life, physical performance, depression, kinesiophobia, and sleep quality in individuals with osteoporotic vertebral fractures. In this single-centre, open-label randomized controlled trial (unblinded), 48 participants with osteoporotic vertebral fractures were randomly allocated (1:1) to an intervention group (n = 24) or a control group (n = 24). Forty-four participants (intervention: 23, control: 21) completed the study. The intervention group received individually supervised, 40-minute exercise sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks, focusing on spinal extensor, postural, lower-extremity strengthening, and balance exercises. Resistance progressed from body weight to external resistance based on individual tolerance, and balance tasks progressed from static to dynamic, with missed sessions rescheduled within the same week. The control group continued usual activities. Pain was assessed using the Short Form McGill Pain Scale, quality of life with the QUALEFFO-41 questionnaire, physical performance with the 6-minute walk test, depression with the Beck Depression Scale (BDS), disability with the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and kinesiophobia with the Tampa Kinesiophobia Scale (TKS). Sleep quality and sleepiness were evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS). Compared with the control group, the intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in VAS pain (mean difference: -1.24, 95% CI: -1.59 to -0.89; p < 0.05) and 6-minute walk distance (38.94 m, 95% CI: 29.59 to 48.28; p < 0.05). Significant improvements favoring the intervention group were also observed for depression (BDS: -4.52, 95% CI: -6.51 to -2.54; p < 0.05), disability (ODI: -2.63, 95% CI: -4.13 to -1.12; p < 0.05), and kinesiophobia (TKS: -10.81, 95% CI: -13.50 to -8.12; p < 0.05) as well as the QUALEFFO-41 total score (p < 0.05). No statistically significant between-group differences were found for sleep quality (PSQI; p = 0.057) or daytime sleepiness (ESS; p = 0.210). A 12-week structured exercise program appears to provide superior benefits in reducing pain and improving functional capacity, depression, and kinesiophobia compared with usual care. These findings suggest that such exercise protocols can be effectively integrated into rehabilitation plans for participants with osteoporotic vertebral fractures, though some elements such as sleep quality may require further investigation. papers.title: Seizure quantification using wearable devices.
papers.abstract: Accurate assessment of seizure occurrence is central to treatment optimization, risk stratification, and management of epilepsy, yet remains largely dependent on patient-reported seizure diaries, which are frequently incomplete and unreliable. Wearable technologies have emerged as promising tools to enable objective and continuous seizure monitoring by capturing seizure-induced physiological signals. Over the past decade, substantial progress has been made in the development and clinical validation of wearable seizure detection systems, particularly for generalized convulsive seizures, where high sensitivity can be achieved, whereas detection of nonconvulsive seizures remains more limited. However, translating detection into clinically meaningful seizure quantification presents important challenges, including variability in performance across seizure types, patient populations, and individual physiological responses, as well as differences between controlled and real-world settings. This narrative review critically examines wearable technologies for seizure quantification, integrating recent clinical evidence and expert perspectives. We discuss key sensor modalities, including accelerometry, electrocardiography-derived features such as heart rate variability, multimodal biosignal integration, and emerging ultra-long-term wearable and subcutaneous electroencephalographic systems. Each modality offers specific advantages and limitations depending on seizure type and clinical context. Attention is also given to the importance of user trust, adherence, and data quality as key determinants of clinical utility. We further examine the role of wearable seizure quantification in clinical practice, including treatment monitoring, tele-epileptology, and clinical trials, as well as potential future contributions to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk assessment. With continued technological advances and robust real-world clinical validation, wearable systems have the potential to transform seizure monitoring and support more precise, data-driven epilepsy care.

papers.title: Two-stage spatiotemporal graph neural network framework for seizure onset zone localization.
papers.abstract: Accurate localization of the seizure onset zone (SOZ) is critical for the presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy. Intracranial electroencephalography captures high-resolution seizure dynamics, but interpreting complex spatiotemporal patterns across implanted electrodes is clinically challenging. We propose a two-stage, uncertainty-aware framework for SOZ localization that integrates patient-specific seizure modeling with cross-patient probabilistic ranking to estimate the likelihood of each electrode belonging to the SOZ. The framework was evaluated on a bi-institutional cohort of 36 patients (20 with good surgical outcome, 16 with poor surgical outcome), comprising 184 seizures. In the first stage, a patient-specific spatiotemporal graph neural network modeled seizure onset as a network-level transition using directed functional connectivity graphs derived from burst-integrated electrophysiological features. Trained solely to detect preictal-to-ictal transitions, this model generated electrode probability trajectories without SOZ supervision. In the second stage, these trajectories were summarized into interpretable descriptors and used to train a patient-agnostic classifier assigning SOZ likelihood scores to electrodes. Evaluation and hyperparameter optimization were performed using nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation restricted to good outcome patients, ensuring strict patient-level separation between training, validation, and test data. Seizure onset detection was stable across patients, with comparable binary cross-entropy values between outcome groups (median = .495 vs. .438, p = .108). In good outcome patients, SOZ electrodes were prioritized among top-ranked contacts (area under the curve = .86 ± .06), with all patients exhibiting at least one SOZ electrode within the top positions. In poor outcome patients, predictions exhibited reduced spatial separability, lower likelihood magnitudes, and near-zero confidence gaps, reflecting attenuated model confidence. This two-stage framework integrates spatial interactions, temporal dynamics, and probabilistic ranking within a pipeline. By providing graded SOZ likelihood estimates and uncertainty-aware prioritization, the approach is a decision-support tool to assist hypothesis refinement during presurgical evaluation rather than as a standalone diagnostic system.
